68	\subsection{Entity Construction as MBR Decoding}\label{sec:mbr_theory}
69	
70	Entity-level construction (\S\ref{sec:selection_method}) is a special case of minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{kumar2004minimum, eikema2020map}, extended from candidate selection ($\arg\max_{y \in \{y_1,\ldots,y_N\}}$) to construction over all subsets of $E_\cup{=}\bigcup_i y_i$.
71	
72	\begin{proposition}[Entity construction as MBR for balanced set-overlap]\label{prop:construction_mbr}
73	Under entity-wise independence with utility $u(\hat{y}, y') = |\hat{y} \cap y'| - \alpha|\hat{y} \setminus y'|$ ($\alpha \geq 1$), the MBR-optimal constructed set is
74	\begin{equation}\label{eq:mbr_construction}
75	\hat{y}_{\textup{MBR}} \!=\! \bigl\{e \!{\in}\! E_\cup \!:\! \hat{p}(e) \!>\! \tfrac{\alpha}{\alpha{+}1}\bigr\},\; \hat{p}(e) \!=\! \tfrac{1}{N} \textstyle\sum\nolimits_{i} \mathbf{1}[e \!{\in}\! y_i]
76	\end{equation}
77	The special case $\alpha{=}1$ yields $\hat{p}(e) > \tfrac{1}{2}$, the majority-vote threshold used throughout (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_proof}).
78	\end{proposition}
79	
80	\noindent\textbf{Remark.}
81	Set-level F1 is non-linear and admits no closed-form threshold rule \cite{dembczynski2011exact}. We use balanced linear utility as a tractable surrogate; empirically the $1/2$ threshold yields F1 within 0.05\,pp of grid-searched optimum for typical NER outputs ($|E_\cup| \leq 30$).
82	
83	Signal-derived weights $w_i$ yield quality-weighted MBR: $\hat{p}_w(e) = \sum_{i} w_i \, \mathbf{1}[e {\in} y_i] / \sum_{i} w_i$, equivalent to self-normalized weighting with quality scores as unnormalized weights.
84	Weighted MBR tends to improve when $w_i$ correlates with $u(y_i, y^*)$ within instances; when this correlation is weak (LP on SciERC: $\rho{\approx}0.2$; few-shot: \S\ref{sec:scaling}), weighting degrades (\S\ref{sec:selection_method}).

Construction fails for all Qwen2.5 configurations on Few-NERD (both n.s.); 3$\to$5 epochs triples degeneracy within the same model (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
210	
211	Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): FewNERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, while SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$); a single stochastic sample underperforms greedy ($N{\geq}4$ needed to match).

\section{MBR Decoding and Entity Construction}\label{app:mbr_discussion}

\subsection{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:construction_mbr}}\label{app:mbr_proof}

We show that under entity-wise independence, the MBR-optimal constructed set with utility $u(\hat{y}, y') = |\hat{y} \cap y'| - \alpha|\hat{y} \setminus y'|$ ($\alpha \geq 1$) includes entity $e$ iff $\hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha+1)$.
Consider constructing $\hat{y} \subseteq E_\cup$ to maximize expected utility against the empirical sample distribution.
Under entity-wise independence, each entity inclusion is an independent binary decision.
For entity $e$ with empirical frequency $\hat{p}(e) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \mathbf{1}[e \in y_i]$, including $e$ contributes $+1$ when $e \in y_i$ (probability $\hat{p}(e)$) and $-\alpha$ when $e \notin y_i$ (probability $1{-}\hat{p}(e)$).
The expected marginal contribution is $\hat{p}(e) - \alpha(1{-}\hat{p}(e)) = (1{+}\alpha)\hat{p}(e) - \alpha$, which is positive iff $\hat{p}(e) > \alpha/(\alpha+1)$.
The special case $\alpha{=}1$ yields the majority-vote threshold $\hat{p}(e) > 1/2$ used throughout.
With F1 utility, the optimal threshold depends on the full probability vector over $E_\cup$ \cite{dembczynski2011exact}; the constant $1/2$ threshold is a close approximation when $|E_\cup|$ is small (typically 5--15 in our experiments).
The independence assumption is approximate but empirically justified by the effectiveness of entity-level voting (\S\ref{sec:selection_method}).

\subsection{Connection to MBR Decoding}\label{app:mbr_connection}

Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.

\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complement to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} yield large gains on reasoning and code generation, but the evidence concentrates on tasks with discrete answers or execution-based verification.
Named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
This challenge generalizes to any \textit{set-valued} structured prediction task where outputs admit partial but not exact overlap.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} test-time scaling via LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 68\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
Oracle F1 scales with $N$ at rates comparable to reasoning tasks ($c{\approx}0.5$; \citealp{brown2024monkeys}), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp of the growing ceiling---a persistent \textit{aggregation gap} that intensifies with model capability as degeneracy rises with training convergence (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
Our diagnosis complements MBR utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals on four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}) spanning a difficulty gradient, using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation, varying $N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$ and model capacity across 4B\textendash 8B fine-tuned and 72B zero-shot regimes.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation as a test-time scaling diagnostic.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (AUPRC 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Failure modes of test-time scaling for structured prediction.}
    For fine-tuned 4B--8B models, LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations) but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.
    The resulting three-step diagnostic (measure degeneracy, assess signal alignment, choose aggregation) provides a reusable protocol for structured test-time scaling (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as a partial mitigation for structured test-time scaling failures.}
    The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level aggregation, adapting entity voting from ensemble NER \cite{florian2003named} to stochastic sampling: under fine-tuning and zero-shot regimes, LP-weighted construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$; survives Holm--Bonferroni, $k{=}57$) and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.004$, $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.20$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complement to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} yield large gains on reasoning and code generation, but the evidence concentrates on tasks with discrete answers or execution-based verification.
Named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
This challenge generalizes to any \textit{set-valued} structured prediction task where outputs admit partial but not exact overlap.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} test-time scaling via LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 68\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
Oracle F1 scales with $N$ at rates comparable to reasoning tasks ($c{\approx}0.5$; \citealp{brown2024monkeys}), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp of the growing ceiling---a persistent \textit{aggregation gap} that intensifies with model capability as degeneracy rises with training convergence (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
Our diagnosis complements MBR utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals on four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}) spanning a difficulty gradient, using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation, varying $N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$ and model capacity across 4B\textendash 8B fine-tuned and 72B zero-shot regimes.

    \item \textbf{Quality estimation as a test-time scaling diagnostic.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).

\subsection{Connection to MBR Decoding}\label{app:mbr_connection}

Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy, the core of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472: 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, and the newly non-tied subset shows a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible. Score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.
